opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Eureka is one I'm really proud of, mostly because it flipped a problem I'd been frustrated with for years.

If you've ever trained a robot with reinforcement learning, you know the dirty secret: the hardest part usually isn't the algorithm, it's the reward function. Somebody, usually a very patient PhD student, sits there hand-crafting the reward, tweaking coefficients, running training overnight, looking at the result, and going "nope, the hand flipped the pen off the table again," and then tweaking it again. It's a black art. It doesn't scale.

So the idea behind Eureka was: what if we let a large language model do that job? We gave GPT-4 the source code of the simulation environment and a plain description of the task, and asked it to write the reward function as actual Python code. Then we ran RL in massively parallel GPU simulation with Isaac Gym, gathered statistics on how training went, and fed that back to the model as a kind of reward reflection. The model then edits its own reward code and tries again. It's an evolutionary loop where the LLM is the mutation operator.

What made me happiest was the results. On a large majority of the tasks we tried, Eureka's rewards beat the ones written by human experts. And we got a five-fingered Shadow Hand to do rapid pen spinning, which is extremely dexterous and something nobody had really pulled off with that kind of fluency before. Watching that hand twirl the pen in simulation was a real "eureka" moment for the team, hence the name.

The deeper reason I like it is philosophical. It's a nice example of what I call a foundation model acting as a teacher for a smaller, specialized policy. The LLM doesn't control the robot directly. It writes code that shapes how another neural network learns. So you get the broad world knowledge and coding ability of a big model combined with the precision and speed of RL in simulation, the two working together. And it's all open source, so people have taken it in directions we didn't anticipate, which is the best thing that can happen to a research project.

r001.rationale: The response says Eureka gives GPT-4 the task description and simulation source code and asks it to write the reward function as Python code for reinforcement-learning robot training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, Eureka is one of those projects I'm really proud of, and I think the reason is that it was the first time we got to see a large language model actually do something that felt like genuine research, not just answering questions. The task we picked was deliberately hard: teach a five-fingered robot hand to spin a pen, the kind of thing you'd see a bored student doing in a lecture hall. That's a really dexterous skill. Even for human roboticists, it's extremely difficult to hand-design a reward function for that. You have to tell the robot what "good" looks like at every timestep, and nobody really knows how to write that down for pen spinning.

So what Eureka does is it has GPT-4 write the reward function. It reads the simulation environment's source code, proposes a reward in Python, and then we train a policy in Isaac Gym, our GPU-accelerated simulator, where you can run tens of thousands of environments in parallel. The training results come back, and the model looks at the statistics, what parts of the reward worked, which ones didn't, and it reflects and rewrites the reward. It's an evolutionary loop, basically, with the LLM as the mutation operator and the simulator as the fitness evaluator. And after a few iterations, it produces rewards that outperform the ones that human experts wrote, on the majority of tasks we tested.

What makes me happy about it isn't just the pen spinning demo, even though that one is fun to watch. It's that it closes a loop that I think is going to be very important for the future of robotics. You have a language model doing the high-level creative work, essentially acting as a scientist, and you have massive simulation compute doing the grunt work of trial and error. Neither one alone would get you there. GPT-4 can't spin a pen, and reinforcement learning without a good reward just flails around. Combined, you get something that looks a lot like how a graduate student actually does research: propose, test, read the results, revise.

And I think that pattern generalizes way beyond rewards. Anything in the robot learning pipeline where a human currently sits in the loop reading logs and tweaking things, that's a candidate for this kind of automation. So Eureka for me is less a paper about pen spinning and more a proof of concept that the foundation model can become the researcher, and compute becomes the lab.

r001.rationale: The response says Eureka has GPT-4 write the reward function, proposes it in Python, and then trains a robot policy using it.

astra-6.text:
What I really like about Eureka is that it connects the reasoning ability of language models with the physical skills of robots. A language model can’t directly tell you how to move every joint to spin a pen, but it can write code for a reward function—a signal that tells the robot what it should try to achieve.

Then we train the robot in simulation, look at how well it does, and feed that feedback back to the language model so it can improve the reward. So you get this iterative loop: propose something, test it, learn from the results.

The exciting part is that the resulting rewards can outperform ones designed by human experts. And they don’t necessarily look like what a human would write. For me, that’s a really compelling example of AI helping us discover how to train another AI, with the results grounded in something you can actually measure and watch.

r001.rationale: The response explains that Eureka uses a language model to write code for a reward function that guides robot training.

sol-6.1.text:
What I love about Eureka is that it connects two very different worlds: language models, which are good at reasoning in code, and robots, which have to learn through interaction with the physical world.

One of the hardest parts of reinforcement learning is designing the reward function. You can tell a robot, “I want you to spin this pen,” but translating that into a mathematical signal that actually produces the behavior takes a lot of trial and error. With Eureka, we have a language model write that reward code, run the learning process, look at feedback, and then improve the reward. So it’s an iterative research loop.

The exciting part is that it can come up with solutions that we wouldn’t necessarily write ourselves. You’re using the language model to help discover how to teach a skill, rather than asking it to directly control every movement. To me, that’s a really compelling way to combine the strengths of language models and reinforcement learning.

r001.rationale: It says Eureka uses a language model to write reward code, then runs the learning process to teach a robot a skill.
